title: A boundary that chooses
question: What is a cell's outer boundary made of, and how did scientists find out?
hook: Scientists worked out the structure of the cell's boundary by spreading its fat on water and measuring.
idea: The cell membrane is a lipid bilayer that controls what moves in and out of a cell.

beats.prompt: Researchers extract all the lipid from red blood cells and spread it in one layer on water. If the cell membrane is a double layer of lipid, how will the spread-out area compare with the cells' surface area?

choices.label: About the same
choices.feedback: That would fit a single layer, but the membrane has two layers, so the lipid covers more.

choices.label: About half as large
choices.feedback: Spreading lipid out cannot make it cover less than the cells' own surface if it was a bilayer.

choices.label: About ten times as large
choices.feedback: The measured ratio was far smaller, about 2:1.

beats.explain: The ratio of the water surface covered to the cells' surface area was approximately 2:1, which led to the bilayer conclusion.

beats.prompt: Put these steps in the story of the cell membrane in order.
items: Overton proposes membranes are made of lipids
Gorter and Grendel propose the lipid bilayer
Singer and Nicolson propose the fluid mosaic model

beats.prompt: Sort each description into the kind of membrane protein it fits.
beats.explain: Integral proteins span the membrane and serve as transporters; peripheral proteins attach to the surface and act as enzymes.

beats.prompt: One step in the reasoning behind the red blood cell experiment is wrong. Which?
steps: Mature mammalian red blood cells lack nuclei and organelles.
So their plasma membrane is their only lipid-containing structure.
So some of the extracted lipid must have come from inside the cells.
So the measured lipid area describes the plasma membrane alone.
beats.explain: With no nucleus or organelles, all extracted lipid can be assumed to have come from the plasma membrane.
